title: Run, price and prove a small security audit

say: Run, price and prove a small security audit.
This is the video for module 3 of Cybersecurity Fundamentals.
When you review someone else's security, the first document is not a technical report. It is written permission.

say: Step one is a signed authorisation from someone with authority. It says what you may look at, which systems, which dates, and what you must not do.
Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act 2015 makes unauthorised access an offence. So never log in, scan or send test phishing without clear written permission for exactly that.

panel.heading: From first call to findings
panel.rule: No written permission, no checking. Ever.

say: Next, interview the leader, then staff and admins. Ask who handles payments, who the admins are, which accounts have two-step verification, and what has gone wrong before.

panel.heading: From first call to findings
panel.rule: No written permission, no checking. Ever.

say: Then check settings together. The owner clicks, you watch and take notes. Passwords stay with their owner.

panel.heading: From first call to findings
panel.rule: No written permission, no checking. Ever.

say: Finally, score each finding with likelihood times impact, as you learned in module 1.

say: For example, Zainab reviews a private primary school in Ibadan with 14 staff email accounts. With the admin officer beside her, she counts 11 accounts with 2-Step Verification. That is about 79%.

say: And the bursar accepts bank changes by email with no call-back. That scores 15.
Each finding is written as a fact, with why it matters, its score, and a fix with an owner and date. No fear language, no blame.

say: Now pricing. Zainab breaks the work into phases: discovery 6 hours, hardening 10, training 4, and report 3. That is 23 hours.
At an illustrative rate of 8,000 naira an hour, the base fee is 184,000 naira.
She adds 15% for unknowns, which is 27,600 naira.
That is 211,600 naira, which she rounds to 212,000. She asks for 50% on signing and 50% when she delivers the report.
Tools the school buys, like a backup drive, are listed separately, not hidden in her fee.
Write both lists. In scope: the 14 staff accounts, the Facebook page settings, backups with one restore test, and the report and incident plan.

panel.heading: What the audit covers
left: Backup set-up and one restore test

say: Out of scope: the bank portal, website testing, and monitoring after handover. And no honest professional can promise that no attack will ever succeed. Promise checkable actions instead.
If the client asks for extra work midway, write it down, quote it, and get approval in writing first.

panel.heading: What the audit covers

say: For example, Ngozi leads security for a 20-person NGO in Port Harcourt. Before training, 9 of 20 staff had 2-Step Verification. That is 45%.

cards.d: 9 of 20 staff had 2-Step Verification: 45%. Staff reported 1 suspicious email that month.
Teach three behaviours only. Staff turn on 2-Step together; 8 more enrol in the room.
One week later: 20 of 20, 100%. Next month staff reported 7 suspicious emails.

say: In her session she teaches three behaviours only: check the real sender, call back on numbers on file, and report anything odd at once. Everyone turns on 2-Step together, and reporting is blame-free.

say: Turn your work into case studies: the situation, what you did, results in numbers, anonymised documents, and a short reference with permission.
Never show passwords, recovery codes, staff names or personal data. Trust is the real product of security work.

To remember. Get written authorisation before any review. Write findings as facts with a score, fix, owner and date. Your fee is hours times rate, plus a stated contingency. Write both scope lists. And measure before and after, so you can show what changed.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Findings: fact, score, fix, owner, date
Fee = hours x rate plus contingency
Write in scope and out of scope
